title: SQL injection in the login
brief: 16:40. A pull request changes the customer portal login. QA says it works. You are the reviewer, and staging is open for you to try it.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: The query is built by gluing strings together, so the input can rewrite the query itself.
teaches: Untrusted input glued into a query becomes part of the query
Parameterised queries keep data and code apart, for good
Escaping by hand and client checks are not fixes; least privilege limits the damage

value.title: Customer portal: login change

lines: const sql = "SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE email = '" + email +

value.intro: Staging runs the branch. Send it a normal sign in first, then try to break it. The email field goes straight into the query.

attempts.label: Sign in as a normal customer
Sign in with a wrong password
Email: admin@veltrix-logistics.com' --  (any password)
attempts.request:
POST /login
{ "email": "admin@veltrix-logistics.com' --", "password": "x" }

Query run:
SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE email = 'admin@veltrix-logistics.com' --' AND pw_hash = '...'

attempts.label: Email: ' OR '1'='1' --

fix.prompt: The cause is that data can change the query. Pick every change that removes that, and any that limits the damage if something else goes wrong.

options.label: Use a parameterised query, with the values passed separately
code: - const sql = "SELECT ... WHERE email = '" + email + "' AND ..."
+   'SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE email = $1 AND pw_hash = $2',
options.why: The database receives the query and the values separately, so a value can never become part of the query. This is the fix.

options.label: Run the portal with a database account that can only read and write what it needs
code: + -- portal_app: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on customer tables only
+ -- no DROP, no access to the admin schema
options.why: Defence in depth: if another injection slips in, it cannot drop tables or read the admin schema.

options.label: Escape single quotes in the email with a replace
options.why: Hand written escaping misses other characters, encodings and other parts of the query. Attackers have been getting round these for twenty years.

options.label: Validate the email format in the browser form
options.why: The attacker does not use your form. They send the request directly, so nothing in the browser stops them.

options.label: Rate limit the login endpoint
options.why: Worth doing, but it slows the attack down. It does not stop it.

setup.title: Workbench
setup.body: Review the login change on staging

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.objective: Reproduce the bug: read the Code tab, then use the Exploit tab on staging.
exploit.insight: The query is built by gluing strings together, so the input can rewrite the query itself.

hint.text: Open the Workbench. Read the code, try normal use on the Exploit tab, then send the request that breaks it.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: Everything after the two dashes was treated as a comment, so the query never checked the password. You are signed in as an admin with no password at all.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: The password check disappeared
body: Everything after the two dashes was treated as a comment, so the query never checked the password. You are signed in as an admin with no password at all.
Look at lines 3 and 4: the email is glued straight into the query. Whatever the user types becomes part of the code.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: With a parameterised query the database gets the query and the values separately. The email can contain quotes, dashes and SQL, and it is only ever a value to compare.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: Data can no longer become code
body: With a parameterised query the database gets the query and the values separately. The email can contain quotes, dashes and SQL, and it is only ever a value to compare.
A restricted database account means that even a future injection somewhere cannot drop tables or read the admin schema.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: Escaping quotes or checking the form in the browser stops the attack you just tried. It does not stop the next one: other characters, other encodings, other fields.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: You blocked one payload, not the bug
body: Escaping quotes or checking the form in the browser stops the attack you just tried. It does not stop the next one: other characters, other encodings, other fields.
Injection is fixed at the cause. Keep data and code apart with parameters.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
